claim: Dendritic cells residing in the skin represent a large family of antigen-presenting cells, ranging from long-lived Langerhans cells (LC) in the epidermis to various distinct classical dendritic cell subsets in the dermis.
source: Dendritic cells residing in the skin represent a large family of antigen-presenting cells, ranging from long-lived Langerhans cells (LC) in the epidermis to various distinct classical dendritic cell subsets in the dermis.
evidence: This is a general statement about skin dendritic cells supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A novel separate population of LC-independent CD207+CD326+ LClike cells exists in the dermis.
source: Through genetic fate mapping analysis and single-cell RNA-sequencing, we have identified a novel separate population of LC-independent CD207+CD326+ LClike cells in the dermis that homed at a slow rate to the lymph nodes (LNs).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic fate mapping analysis and single-cell RNA-sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LClike cells home at a slow rate to the lymph nodes.
source: Through genetic fate mapping analysis and single-cell RNA-sequencing, we have identified a novel separate population of LC-independent CD207+CD326+ LClike cells in the dermis that homed at a slow rate to the lymph nodes (LNs).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from fate mapping studies.

claim: LClike cells are long-lived and radio-resistant.
source: These LClike cells are long-lived and radio-resistant but, unlike LCs, they are gradually replenished by bone marrow-derived precursors under steady state.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera experiments and fate mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LClike cells are gradually replenished by bone marrow-derived precursors under steady state, unlike LCs.
source: These LClike cells are long-lived and radio-resistant but, unlike LCs, they are gradually replenished by bone marrow-derived precursors under steady state.
evidence: This is demonstrated through fate mapping experiments showing gradual replacement over time.

claim: LClike cells together with cDC1s are the main migratory CD207+CD326+ cell fractions present in the LN.
source: LClike cells together with cDC1s are the main migratory CD207+CD326+ cell fractions present in the LN and not, as currently assumed, LCs, which are barely detectable, if at all.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis of lymph node populations shown in Figure 1.

claim: LCs are barely detectable in the lymph nodes, if at all.
source: LClike cells together with cDC1s are the main migratory CD207+CD326+ cell fractions present in the LN and not, as currently assumed, LCs, which are barely detectable, if at all.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis showing absence of F4/80hiCD11bhi LCs in LN.

claim: Cutaneous tolerance to haptens depends on LClike cells.
source: Cutaneous tolerance to haptens depends on LClike cells, whereas LCs suppress effector CD8+ T-cell functions and inflammation locally in the skin during contact hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by tolerance experiments using different DTR mouse strains shown in Figure 8.

claim: LCs suppress effector CD8+ T-cell functions and inflammation locally in the skin during contact hypersensitivity.
source: Cutaneous tolerance to haptens depends on LClike cells, whereas LCs suppress effector CD8+ T-cell functions and inflammation locally in the skin during contact hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CHS experiments in DC-SIGN DTR mice showing enhanced inflammation in absence of LCs.

claim: Paul Langerhans described a novel dendritic-shaped, non-pigmentary cell population in the epidermis in 1868.
source: In 1868, Paul Langerhans described a novel dendritic-shaped, non-pigmentary cell population in the epidermis (Langerhans, 1868).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Langerhans' original work.

claim: Langerhans cells were first classified as cellular members of the nervous system due to their morphological similarity with neurons.
source: These so-called Langerhans cells (LCs) were first classified as cellular members of the nervous system, due to their morphological similarity with neurons.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the initial classification of LCs.

claim: It became clear in the 1980s that Langerhans cells belonged to the dendritic cell family.
source: It was not until the 1980s when it became clear that this peculiar epidermal cell fraction with its potent antigen presentation activity belonged to the dendritic cell (DC) family (Romani and Schuler, 1989; Schuler and Steinman, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to seminal papers from the 1980s.

claim: LCs are generally considered as epidermal tissue-resident macrophages due to their dependence on CSF1, their embryonic origin and local self-maintenance.
source: Despite the fact that LCs share many features with DCs, they are generally considered as epidermal tissue-resident macrophages, mainly due to their dependence on CSF1, their embryonic origin and local self-maintenance (Wynn et al., 2013), although a conventional 'macrophage signature' (e.g. CD16/32, CD64, and MerTK expression) is missing (Gautier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on LC characteristics.

claim: LCs lack a conventional macrophage signature (e.g. CD16/32, CD64, and MerTK expression).
source: Despite the fact that LCs share many features with DCs, they are generally considered as epidermal tissue-resident macrophages, mainly due to their dependence on CSF1, their embryonic origin and local self-maintenance (Wynn et al., 2013), although a conventional 'macrophage signature' (e.g. CD16/32, CD64, and MerTK expression) is missing (Gautier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gautier et al., 2012.

claim: LCs can sense invading pathogens and initiate an intrinsic maturation process that drives their migration out of the epidermis.
source: LCs can sense invading pathogens and initiate an intrinsic maturation process that drives their migration out of the epidermis (Romani et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Romani et al., 2001.

claim: LCs have been regarded as a prototype antigen-presenting cell that can migrate to draining lymph nodes to initiate an immune response by priming naïve LN-resident T-cells.
source: As such, LCs have been regarded as a prototype antigen-presenting cell (APC) (Nagao et al., 2009) that can, after antigen capture, migrate to the draining lymph nodes (LNs) to initiate an immune response by priming naïve LN-resident T-cells (Romani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antigen presentation can occur in skin-draining LNs independently of LCs.
source: Antigen presentation can, however, occur in skin-draining LNs independently of LCs (Henri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henri et al., 2010.

claim: The skin hosts several distinct dermal DC subpopulations.
source: In fact, the skin hosts several other distinct dermal DC subpopulations (Henri et al., 2010; Kissenpfennig et al., 2005), the presence of which complicates the analysis of the cellular contribution to skin immune responses, such as contact hypersensitivity (CHS).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Henri et al., 2010 and Kissenpfennig et al., 2005.

claim: CD326+CD207+ LCs are predominantly found within the CD11bhiF4/80hi fraction in the epidermis.
source: In the epidermis, we confirmed that CD326+CD207+ LCs are predominantly found within the CD11bhiF4/80hi fraction (Nagao et al., 2009; Valladeau et al., 2000; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is confirmed by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: A fraction of CD11bhiF4/80hi cells in the dermis co-expressed CD326 and CD207.
source: In the dermis, we found a fraction of CD11bhiF4/80hi cells that co-expressed CD326 and CD207 (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The remaining dermal CD11bhiF4/80hi cells were CD326-CD207- tissue-resident macrophages.
source: As expected, the remaining dermal CD11bhiF4/80hi cells were CD326-CD207- tissue-resident macrophages (Sheng et al., 2015; Tamoutounour et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dermal DCs were localized in the F4/80int and CD11chiMHCII+ DC fraction.
source: Dermal DCs were localized in the F4/80int and CD11chiMHCII+ DC fraction, which we could separate into three subpopulations based on CD103 and CD11b expression: CD103+CD11b- (defined as cDC1), CD103-CD11blow, and CD103-CD11bhi (defined as CD11bhi).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CD103+CD11b- DCs but not CD103-CD11bhi DCs co-expressed CD326 and CD207.
source: CD103+CD11b- DCs but not CD103-CD11bhi DCs co-expressed CD326 and CD207.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1B.

claim: The CD103-CD11blow subpopulation can be divided into CD326-CD207- (TN) and CD326+CD207+ (LClike) fractions.
source: We could also divide the CD103-CD11blow subpopulation into CD326-CD207- (defined as triple negative [TN]) and CD326+CD207+ (defined as LClike) fractions (Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sirpa is expressed on dermal LCs, LClike, TN, and CD11bhi DCs, while dermal CD103+ DCs lack this receptor.
source: The signal regulatory protein α (Sirpa), a myeloid cell-specific receptor, was expressed on dermal LCs, LClike, TN, and CD11bhi DCs, while, as expected, dermal CD103+ DCs lacked this receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), result validated also by the single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis shown later (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Dermal LCs and LClike cells express similar levels of CD80 and CD86.
source: In terms of costimulatory receptors, dermal LCs and LClike cells express similar levels of CD80 and CD86, whereas the remaining DC subpopulations display lower levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bona fide epidermal and dermal LCs showing the F4/80hiCD11bhi phenotype were not detected in the LN.
source: Notably, we did not detect the bona fide epidermal and dermal LCs showing the original F4/80hiCD11bhi phenotype in the LN (Figure 1C, right, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The CD11bhi DC fraction represented the largest DC subpopulation in the dermis.
source: In agreement with previous work (Henri et al., 2010), the CD11bhi DC fraction represented the largest DC subpopulation in the dermis, whereas in the LN all four DC subpopulations (CD11bhi, cDC1, TN, and LClike) were almost equally represented (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by frequency analysis shown in Figure 1D and supported by citation.

claim: In the LN all four DC subpopulations (CD11bhi, cDC1, TN, and LClike) were almost equally represented.
source: In agreement with previous work (Henri et al., 2010), the CD11bhi DC fraction represented the largest DC subpopulation in the dermis, whereas in the LN all four DC subpopulations (CD11bhi, cDC1, TN, and LClike) were almost equally represented (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by frequency analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nine different cell clusters could be identified in the dermis by unsupervised clustering: LC, LClike, mast cells/neutrophils, DC/monocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes 1, lymphocytes 2, mesenchymal cells, and epithelial cells.
source: Nine different cell clusters could be broadly identified by unsupervised clustering and classified as follows: (1) LC, (2) LClike, (3) mast cells/neutrophils, (4) DC/monocytes, (5) macrophages, (6) lymphocytes 1, (7) lymphocytes 2, (8) mesenchymal cells, and (9) epithelial cells.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Conventional DC, monocyte, and other myeloid-related signature genes are mainly detectable in the DC/mono and mast cell/neutrophil clusters and are mainly absent or weakly expressed in the LC/LClike clusters.
source: Conventional DCs, monocytes, and other myeloid-related signature genes, such as Zbtb46 (DCs), Xcr1 and Clec9a (cDC1), Siglech (plasmacytoid DC), Ly6c and Ccr2 (monocytes), Gata2 and Fcer1a (mast cells), and Ly6g (neutrophils), are mainly detectable in the DC/mono and mast cell/neutrophil clusters (3–4) and are mainly absent or weakly expressed in the LC/LClike clusters (1–2) (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells are detected in LC, LClike, and DC/monocyte clusters.
source: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells are detected in LC (1), LClike (2), as well as in DC/monocyte cluster (4), which confirms the presence of three distinct CD207+CD326+ dermal subpopulations observed by flow cytometry (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data and confirms flow cytometry observations.

claim: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells in cluster 4 co-express Clec9a, Xcr1, Irf8 and represent cDC1s.
source: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells detected in the cluster 4 are co-expressing Clec9a, Xcr1, Irf8 hence they represent the cDC1s (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data showing co-expression of cDC1 markers.

claim: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells in LC and LClike clusters share many previously reported LC signature genes.
source: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells in clusters 1 (LC) and 2 (LClike) share many of the previously reported LC signature genes (e.g. Cd11c, Adgre1, Cd74, Mafb, Pu.1, Csf1r, Tgfbr1) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but several other genes are differentially expressed in LClike cells (e.g. Tgfbr2, Sylt3, Col27a1, Fernt2, Spry2) or in LC cells (e.g. Cd209a, Agpat4, Birc3, Dusp16, Gdpd3, Ly75 and Ppfibp2), respectively (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several genes are differentially expressed between LClike cells and LC cells.
source: Cd207 and Cd326 expressing cells in clusters 1 (LC) and 2 (LClike) share many of the previously reported LC signature genes (e.g. Cd11c, Adgre1, Cd74, Mafb, Pu.1, Csf1r, Tgfbr1) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but several other genes are differentially expressed in LClike cells (e.g. Tgfbr2, Sylt3, Col27a1, Fernt2, Spry2) or in LC cells (e.g. Cd209a, Agpat4, Birc3, Dusp16, Gdpd3, Ly75 and Ppfibp2), respectively (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: There is a close relationship between LC and LClike cells based on developmental trajectory analysis.
source: Clearly there is a close relationship between LC and LClike as well as between macrophages/monocytes and CD11b+/TN DCs, whereas cDC1s are identified as a separate independent cell cluster (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP developmental trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: cDC1s are identified as a separate independent cell cluster from LC and LClike cells.
source: Clearly there is a close relationship between LC and LClike as well as between macrophages/monocytes and CD11b+/TN DCs, whereas cDC1s are identified as a separate independent cell cluster (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: LC and LClike cells share many transcription factors, some equally expressed (Mafb, Irf4, Irf8), some higher expressed in LC (Pu.1), and some more elevated in LClike (Stat3, Runx2, Runx3, Id2, Klf4, Maf).
source: Furthermore, detailed transcription factor (TF) analysis revealed that LC and LClike cells share many TFs, some equally expressed (Mafb, Irf4, Irf8), some higher expressed in LC (Pu.1), and some more elevated in LClike (Stat3, Runx2, Runx3, Id2, Klf4, Maf) (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transcription factor analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Zbtb46 is expressed on both LC and LClike cells but not as high as on classical DCs.
source: Zbtb46, a TF selectively expressed on classical DCs, is expressed on both LC and LClike cells but not as high as on classical DCs (cDC1, CD11b+, and TN) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Zeb2 is only weakly expressed on LC and LClike cells.
source: Interestingly, Zeb2, a specific cDC2 TF, is only weakly expressed on LC and LClike cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LC-related genes such as Mmp9, Cd9, Mfge8, Cldn1 are elevated in dermal LCs and weakly expressed in dermal LClike cells.
source: Furthermore, LC-related genes, such as Mmp9, Cd9, Mfge8, Cldn1 (Ferrer et al., 2019; Miyasaka et al., 2004; Ratzinger et al., 2002; Zimmerli and Hauser, 2007), are elevated in dermal LCs and weakly expressed in dermal LClike cells (Figure 3D), whereas no substantial differences are detected in expression of Sirpa, Ccr7, and Cd24a (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D and supported by citations.

claim: No substantial differences are detected in expression of Sirpa, Ccr7, and Cd24a between LC and LClike cells.
source: Furthermore, LC-related genes, such as Mmp9, Cd9, Mfge8, Cldn1 (Ferrer et al., 2019; Miyasaka et al., 2004; Ratzinger et al., 2002; Zimmerli and Hauser, 2007), are elevated in dermal LCs and weakly expressed in dermal LClike cells (Figure 3D), whereas no substantial differences are detected in expression of Sirpa, Ccr7, and Cd24a (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: F4/80 expression is reduced in LClike cells compared to LCs.
source: The reduced expression of Adgre1 (F4/80) in LClike cells (Figure 3E), re-confirms the downregulation of F4/80 surface expression on this cell type observed in our previous flow cytometry analysis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E and confirmed by flow cytometry in Figure 1.

claim: Both β and γ chains of the IL-2R (Il2rb and Il2rg) are highly expressed in LClike cells, whereas LCs express the lowest levels among different DCs and macrophages subpopulations.
source: Interestingly, both β and γ chains of the IL-2R (Il2rb and Il2rg), previously reported to be expressed in DCs (Zelante et al., 2012), are highly expressed in LClike cells, whereas LCs are the dermal cells expressing the lowest levels among the different DCs and macrophages subpopulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and supported by citation.

claim: Epidermal LCs derived partially from primitive yolk sac progenitors.
source: Fate mapping experiments have shown that epidermal LCs derived partially from primitive yolk sac progenitors (Hoeffel et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015); therefore, the developmental origin of LCs is distinct from conventional DCs and resembled more microglia.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The developmental origin of LCs is distinct from conventional DCs and resembles more microglia.
source: Fate mapping experiments have shown that epidermal LCs derived partially from primitive yolk sac progenitors (Hoeffel et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015); therefore, the developmental origin of LCs is distinct from conventional DCs and resembled more microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the yolk sac origin shared with microglia.

claim: About 12% of epidermal LCs were YFP labelled in E7.5 KitMerCreMer/R26 fate mapping mice, confirming their partial yolk sac origin.
source: However, about 12% of epidermal LCs were YFP labelled, confirming their partial yolk sac origin (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data shown in Figure 4C and F.

claim: Dermal LC counterparts showed similar YFP labelling profile (~10%) to epidermal LCs in E7.5 fate mapping.
source: In comparison, the dermal LC counterparts showed a similar labelling profile (~10%), whereas the remaining dermal DC subpopulations (LClike, cDC1, CD11bhi, and TN) showed a significantly lower 5% YFP signal, very likely, attributed to small spillover of labelling in the HSCs (haematopoietic stem cells) (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: The remaining dermal DC subpopulations (LClike, cDC1, CD11bhi, and TN) showed a significantly lower 5% YFP signal in E7.5 fate mapping, likely attributed to small spillover of labelling in the HSCs.
source: In comparison, the dermal LC counterparts showed a similar labelling profile (~10%), whereas the remaining dermal DC subpopulations (LClike, cDC1, CD11bhi, and TN) showed a significantly lower 5% YFP signal, very likely, attributed to small spillover of labelling in the HSCs (haematopoietic stem cells) (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data shown in Figure 4D and F, with interpretation of spillover.

claim: Yolk sac only contributed to LCs but not to dermal LClike cells.
source: Therefore, YS only contributed to LCs but not to dermal LClike cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the E7.5 fate mapping data showing differential labeling.

claim: LCs are the only cell type from the DC family that originate from self-renewing radio-resistant embryonic precursors.
source: LCs are the only cell type from the DC family that originate from self-renewing radio-resistant embryonic precursors (Merad et al., 2002); other DC subpopulations are short-lived and constantly replenished by BM progenitors (Kissenpfennig et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other DC subpopulations are short-lived and constantly replenished by BM progenitors.
source: LCs are the only cell type from the DC family that originate from self-renewing radio-resistant embryonic precursors (Merad et al., 2002); other DC subpopulations are short-lived and constantly replenished by BM progenitors (Kissenpfennig et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kissenpfennig et al., 2005.

claim: In the epidermis and dermis, LCs were mostly CD45.2+ and retained their host origins due to local self-renewal in BM chimeras.
source: In the epidermis and dermis, LCs were mostly CD45.2+, and thus retained their host origins due to local self-renewal (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Dermal cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi DCs exhibited a wholly CD45.1+ phenotype after just 1 month following reconstitution in BM chimeras.
source: By contrast, dermal cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi DCs exhibited a wholly CD45.1+ phenotype after just 1 month following reconstitution; this finding means that they are fully BM-derived.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Only LClike cells showed a mixed contribution from both CD45.2+ host and CD45.1+ donor cells in BM chimeras.
source: Only LClike cells showed a mixed contribution from both CD45.2+ host and CD45.1+ donor cells. In fact, after 1 month following reconstitution, only a minority (~10%) of LClike cells were replenished by CD45.1+ cells; this percentage increased to ~50% by 4 months after reconstitution (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: After 1 month following reconstitution, only a minority (~10%) of LClike cells were replenished by CD45.1+ cells; this percentage increased to ~50% by 4 months after reconstitution.
source: Only LClike cells showed a mixed contribution from both CD45.2+ host and CD45.1+ donor cells. In fact, after 1 month following reconstitution, only a minority (~10%) of LClike cells were replenished by CD45.1+ cells; this percentage increased to ~50% by 4 months after reconstitution (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: In skin-draining LNs, cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi cells were mostly derived from donor CD45.1+ BM cells in chimeras.
source: In skin-draining LNs, we found that cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi cells were mostly derived from donor CD45.1+ BM cells, excluding their origins from the radio-resistant LC population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The LClike cell fraction in LN was split into donor CD45.1+ and host CD45.2+ cells in chimeras.
source: Comparable to its dermal counterpart, only the LClike cell fraction was split into donor CD45.1+ and host CD45.2+ cells, respectively (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The contribution of CD45.1+ donor cells to LClike cells in LN increased over time, from ~10% after 1 month to ~45% after 4 months.
source: In addition, the contribution of CD45.1+ donor cells increased over time, from ~10% after 1 month to ~45% after 4 months.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BM chimera data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The unique temporal replacement of LClike cells suggests a dual origin, distinguishing this DC fraction from both conventional long-lived radio-resistant self-renewing LCs and short-lived BM-derived DCs.
source: This unique temporal replacement suggests a dual origin for LClike cells, distinguishing this DC fraction from both conventional long-lived radio-resistant self-renewing LCs and short-lived BM-derived DCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the BM chimera data showing gradual replacement kinetics.

claim: CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells clustered separately but in close proximity in UMAP analysis.
source: Both CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells were clearly visible and clustered separately, but in close proximity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells have ~85% of their gene expression overlapping.
source: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance, complete linkage) and principal component analysis (PCA) analysis revealed that both CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells clustered closely together (not shown), with ~85% of their gene expression overlapping (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The high level of similarity between resident and BM-derived LClike fractions indicates that the microenvironment, and not the cellular origin, seems to determine the LClike cell identity.
source: The high level of similarity between resident and BM-derived LClike fractions indicates that the microenvironment, and not the cellular origin, seems to determine the LClike cell identity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq data showing high similarity between CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells.

claim: cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi DCs were fully labelled with YFP after just 1 month and the labelling was maintained for 8 months in KitMerCreMer/R26 fate mapping mice.
source: cDC1, TN, and CD11bhi DCs, however, were fully labelled with YFP after just 1 month and the labelling was maintained for the remaining 8 months. This finding is consistent with the fast turnover rate identified for these three DC subsets.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: LClike cells gradually accumulated the YFP label from 10% to 60% over the 8-month chase period in KitMerCreMer/R26 fate mapping mice.
source: By contrast, LClike cells gradually accumulated the label from 10% to 60% over the 8-month chase period, supporting that dermis-resident LClike DCs are replaced slowly by BM progenitors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Dermis-resident LClike DCs are replaced slowly by BM progenitors.
source: By contrast, LClike cells gradually accumulated the label from 10% to 60% over the 8-month chase period, supporting that dermis-resident LClike DCs are replaced slowly by BM progenitors.
evidence: This is concluded from the gradual YFP labeling kinetics in fate mapping experiments.

claim: The LClike subset exhibited higher proliferating capability than LC and other DC subsets based on cell cycle analysis.
source: The LClike subset exhibited higher proliferating capability than LC and other DC subsets, consistent with the previous findings that LCs are dividing extremely slow (Ginhoux and Merad, 2010) and conventional DCs do not proliferate in tissues and mainly depend on their BM progenitors for expansion (Liu and Nussenzweig, 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: LCs are dividing extremely slow.
source: The LClike subset exhibited higher proliferating capability than LC and other DC subsets, consistent with the previous findings that LCs are dividing extremely slow (Ginhoux and Merad, 2010) and conventional DCs do not proliferate in tissues and mainly depend on their BM progenitors for expansion (Liu and Nussenzweig, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ginhoux and Merad, 2010.

claim: Conventional DCs do not proliferate in tissues and mainly depend on their BM progenitors for expansion.
source: The LClike subset exhibited higher proliferating capability than LC and other DC subsets, consistent with the previous findings that LCs are dividing extremely slow (Ginhoux and Merad, 2010) and conventional DCs do not proliferate in tissues and mainly depend on their BM progenitors for expansion (Liu and Nussenzweig, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu and Nussenzweig, 2010.

claim: LClike cells displayed slower turnover kinetics than other DC subpopulations and higher proliferating capability to refill the emigration gap.
source: Overall, we showed that LClike cells displayed slower turnover kinetics than other DC subpopulations and higher proliferating capability to refill the emigration gap.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on fate mapping and cell cycle data.

claim: DC-SIGN (CD209a) specific mRNA is present in murine LCs and CD11bhi DCs, but not in cDC1, TN DCs, or LClike cells.
source: Although not detectable by flow cytometry on the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), we measured DC-SIGN (or CD209a) specific mRNA levels in murine LCs as well as in CD11bhi DCs, the latter already known to express this receptor (Cheong et al., 2010), whereas cDC1, TN DCs, or LClike cells were negative (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), a result which was corroborated by the scRNA analysis of dermal cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR and scRNA-seq data, supported by citation.

claim: HBEGF mRNA was detected only in LC isolated from epidermis of DC-SIGN DTR mice and was absent in LCs obtained from WT mice.
source: Accordingly, HBEGF mRNA was detected only in LC isolated from epidermis of DC-SIGN DTR mice and was absent in LCs obtained from WT mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No DC-SIGN downregulation was observed in activated LCs.
source: Clearly no Cd209a downregulation was observed in activated LCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C); therefore, an eventual transition from maturing dermal DC-SIGNpos LCs to dermal DC-SIGNneg LClike cells can be excluded.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis of stimulated vs unstimulated LCs shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An eventual transition from maturing dermal DC-SIGNpos LCs to dermal DC-SIGNneg LClike cells can be excluded.
source: Clearly no Cd209a downregulation was observed in activated LCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C); therefore, an eventual transition from maturing dermal DC-SIGNpos LCs to dermal DC-SIGNneg LClike cells can be excluded.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of DC-SIGN downregulation upon LC activation.

claim: LCs were efficiently depleted in both the epidermis and dermis by short-term and long-term DT treatment protocols in DC-SIGN DTR mice.
source: In the DT-treated DC-SIGN DTR mice, LCs were efficiently depleted in both the epidermis and dermis by the short-term and long-term depletion protocols (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Cells in the CD11bhi cell fraction were affected by DT treatment in DC-SIGN DTR mice, particularly during the short-term depletion protocol where cell numbers were reduced by ~80%.
source: We also found that cells in the CD11bhi cell fraction were affected by the DT treatment; this was particularly evident during the short-term depletion protocol, in which the cell numbers were reduced by ~80% (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: cDC1, TN, and LClike cell numbers were unaffected by DT treatment in DC-SIGN DTR mice and were comparable between DT-injected WT and DC-SIGN mouse strains.
source: Importantly, cDC1, TN, and LClike cell numbers were unaffected and thus were comparable between DT-injected WT and DC-SIGN mouse strains. These results strongly support the independency of LClike cells from classical bona fide epidermal LCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The independency of LClike cells from classical bona fide epidermal LCs is strongly supported by DC-SIGN DTR depletion experiments.
source: Importantly, cDC1, TN, and LClike cell numbers were unaffected and thus were comparable between DT-injected WT and DC-SIGN mouse strains. These results strongly support the independency of LClike cells from classical bona fide epidermal LCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the selective depletion of LCs without affecting LClike cells.

claim: In absence of LC, the replenishment of LClike cells by BM-derived cells is not affected.
source: Although epidermal LCs were absent over the whole period, the YFP labelling profiles of skin-derived LN DC subsets, including the LClike fraction, were comparable between DT-injected DC-SIGN DTR+-KitMerCreMer/R26 and DC-SIGN DTRneg-KitMerCreMer/R26 mice (Figure 7E,F). These data show that in absence of LC, the replenishment of LClike cells by BM-derived cells is not affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping data in LC-depleted mice shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: In absence of LCs, a pronounced increased ear swelling persisted over 10 days in CHS experiments.
source: In absence of LCs, clearly a pronounced increased ear swelling persisted over 10 days (Figure 8B), a phenotype which was already reported in other LC-ablating transgenic mouse strains such as human langerin-DTA (hu-DTA) and human langerin-DTR (huDTR) mice (Kaplan et al., 2005; Bobr et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CHS data shown in Figure 8B and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β were significantly upregulated in ears of DT-treated DC-SIGN DTR mice during CHS.
source: Proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β were clearly significantly upregulated in ears of DT-treated DC-SIGN DTR mice (Figure 8C, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: VEGFα was augmented in absence of LCs during CHS.
source: VEGFα, a biomarker for keratinocyte impairment (Canavese et al., 2010, Bae et al., 2015), was also clearly augmented in absence of LCs (Figure 8C, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 8C and supported by citations.

claim: Higher IFN-γ levels were measured in ears lacking LCs during CHS.
source: In addition, higher IFN-γ levels were measured in ears lacking LCs (Figure 8C, lower panel), values that correlated with an augmented CD8+ T-cell-dependent IFN-γ response observed by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: No major difference was observed in activated dermal ICOS+ Tregs in presence or absence of LCs during CHS.
source: In accordance with previously published data (Igyarto et al., 2009), no major difference was observed in activated dermal ICOS+ Tregs in presence or absence of LCs (Figure 8D, right panel, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8D and supported by citation.

claim: CD207-DTR mice were not tolerized against DNFB and showed robust ear inflammation over time.
source: CD207-DTR mice were clearly not tolerized against DNFB, since they showed robust ear inflammation over time. Such ear swelling was not observed in DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tolerance assay data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice did not show ear swelling upon DNFB challenge.
source: CD207-DTR mice were clearly not tolerized against DNFB, since they showed robust ear inflammation over time. Such ear swelling was not observed in DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tolerance assay data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: A low IFN-γ-producing CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell response was restricted to DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice.
source: In line with the observed ear swelling profile, we found that a low IFN-γ-producing CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell response was restricted to DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice. This response was comparatively enhanced in CD207-DTR and WT mice (Figure 8G, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The diminished level of ear inflammation in DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice correlated with an increased presence of activated ICOS+CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs in the LN.
source: The diminished level of ear inflammation in DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice correlated with an increased presence of activated ICOS+CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs in the LN, which exhibit suppressive activity in CHS to DNFB (Vocanson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8H and supported by citation.

claim: ICOS+CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs exhibit suppressive activity in CHS to DNFB.
source: The diminished level of ear inflammation in DNTB-tolerized WT, Clec9A-DTR, and DC-SIGN-DTR mice correlated with an increased presence of activated ICOS+CD4+FOXP3+ Tregs in the LN, which exhibit suppressive activity in CHS to DNFB (Vocanson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vocanson et al., 2010.

claim: Only LClike cells critically contribute to tolerance induction based on comparison between CD207-DTR, DC-SIGN DTR, and Clec9A-DTR mice.
source: Because of this clear difference between CD207-DTR mice (that lack CD207+ LCs/LC-like cells and CD207+ DC1s) and DC-SIGN DTR mice (that lack only CD207+ LCs) and Clec9A-DTR mice (that lack only CD207+ cDC1), we conclude that only LClike cells critically contribute to tolerance induction.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing tolerance phenotypes across different DTR mouse strains.

claim: Under steady-state conditions, LCs most likely do not exit the skin, or if so, in very low numbers.
source: Here, we demonstrate that under steady-state conditions, LCs most likely do not exit the skin, or if so, in very low numbers.
evidence: This is concluded from the absence of F4/80hiCD11bhi LCs in lymph nodes.

claim: The originally described LN LC fraction is actually an independent LClike cell population that originates from the dermis, not from the epidermis.
source: Through a combined use of genetic fate mapping and novel inducible LC-ablating mouse models, we show that the originally described LN LC fraction is actually an independent LClike cell population that originates from the dermis, not from the epidermis.
evidence: This is concluded from fate mapping and LC depletion experiments.

claim: LClike cells are ontogenitically different from LCs.
source: These LClike cells are ontogenitically different from LCs and are replaced over time by bone marrow (BM)-derived cells with slow kinetics before trafficking to the LN.
evidence: This is concluded from yolk sac fate mapping and BM chimera experiments.

claim: Under steady-state conditions, due to the structural integrity of the basement membrane, epidermal LCs are sessile with static and almost immobile dendrites.
source: Corroborating evidence for differential migratory behaviours among different skin DCs was provided by real-time intravital two-photon microscopy. Under steady-state conditions, due to the structural integrity of the basement membrane, epidermal LCs are sessile with static and almost immobile dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to intravital microscopy studies.

claim: Dermal DC subpopulations are actively crawling through the dermal interstitial space at high velocity even in absence of inflammation.
source: In contrast, dermal DC subpopulations are actively crawling through the dermal interstitial space at high velocity even in absence of inflammation suggesting that continuous migration to LN is a steady-state property of dermal DCs and not epidermal LCs (Ng et al., 2008; Shklovskaya et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to intravital microscopy studies.

claim: Continuous migration to LN is a steady-state property of dermal DCs and not epidermal LCs.
source: In contrast, dermal DC subpopulations are actively crawling through the dermal interstitial space at high velocity even in absence of inflammation suggesting that continuous migration to LN is a steady-state property of dermal DCs and not epidermal LCs (Ng et al., 2008; Shklovskaya et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from intravital microscopy observations cited.

claim: Similar to resident macrophages in tissues such as skin, gut, kidney, and heart, LClike cells have a dual origin involving both embryonic and adult haematopoiesis.
source: Similar to resident macrophages in tissues, such as skin, gut, kidney, and heart, LClike cells have a dual origin involving both embryonic (but not yolk sack-like LCs) and adult haematopoiesis (Molawi et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2015; Soncin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Fetal-derived and BM-derived LClike cells co-exist together in adult tissue and show high similarity despite different origins.
source: These fetal-derived and BM-derived LClike cells co-exist together in adult tissue, and although derived from different origins, they show high similarity. This finding suggests that it is the local tissue microenvironment and not the cellular origin that shapes their final identity.
evidence: This is concluded from RNA-seq data showing high similarity between CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ LClike cells.

claim: The local tissue microenvironment and not the cellular origin shapes the final identity of LClike cells.
source: These fetal-derived and BM-derived LClike cells co-exist together in adult tissue, and although derived from different origins, they show high similarity. This finding suggests that it is the local tissue microenvironment and not the cellular origin that shapes their final identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the high similarity between fetal-derived and BM-derived LClike cells.

claim: A langerin-expressing dermal myeloid CD1+ DC fraction unrelated to XCR1+ DCs and LCs has been reported in human dermis.
source: Similarly, a langerin-expressing dermal myeloid CD1+ DC fraction unrelated to XCR1+ DCs and LCs has been reported in human dermis (Bigley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bigley et al., 2015.

claim: It is likely that the human langerin-expressing dermal myeloid CD1+ DCs are the LClike cells described in this study.
source: It is likely that these cells are the LClike cells described here and further studies will be needed to analyse the potential relationship between murine CD207+ LClike cells and human myeloid CD207+ DC counterparts.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between murine and human cell populations.

claim: All dermal DCs migrate into LNs in a CCR7-dependent fashion.
source: Although all dermal DCs migrate into LNs in a CCR7-dependent fashion (Förster et al., 1999), LClike cells seem to migrate at slower rate than other DCs under steady-state conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Förster et al., 1999.

claim: LClike cells seem to migrate at slower rate than other DCs under steady-state conditions.
source: Although all dermal DCs migrate into LNs in a CCR7-dependent fashion (Förster et al., 1999), LClike cells seem to migrate at slower rate than other DCs under steady-state conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the slow accumulation of LClike cells in LN over time in fate mapping experiments.

claim: Previously reported slow migratory cells originally attributed to LCs are in fact LClike cells.
source: Similar slow trafficking dynamics was originally attributed to LCs (Bursch et al., 2007; Ruedl et al., 2000) but we now strongly believe that these previously reported slow migratory cells are in fact LClike cells.
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of previous findings based on the current study's data.

claim: The genetic fate mapping approach does not support the established paradigm of LCs as being the main 'prototype' migrating APCs to draining LNs under homeostatic conditions.
source: In summary, our genetic fate mapping approach, used to delineate the complex skin DC network, does not support the established paradigm of LCs as being the main 'prototype' migrating APCs to draining LNs under homeostatic conditions (Wilson and Villadangos, 2004).
evidence: This is concluded from the absence of LCs in LN and presence of LClike cells.

claim: LCs at steady state, similar to other tissue-resident macrophages, are sessile and act locally in the skin.
source: We propose, rather, that LCs at steady state, similar to other tissue-resident macrophages, are sessile and act locally in the skin, whereas dermal LClike cells assume many of the functions previously attributed to LCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Dermal LClike cells assume many of the functions previously attributed to LCs.
source: We propose, rather, that LCs at steady state, similar to other tissue-resident macrophages, are sessile and act locally in the skin, whereas dermal LClike cells assume many of the functions previously attributed to LCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on tolerance experiments showing LClike cells mediate tolerance.

claim: The identification of the novel migratory dermal LClike subpopulation opens new avenues in the development of treatments to cure diseases such as contact allergic dermatitis and other inflammatory skin disorders like psoriasis.
source: The identification of this novel migratory dermal LClike subpopulation opens new avenues and approaches in the development of treatments to cure diseases such as contact allergic dermatitis and other inflammatory skin disorders like psoriasis.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.
